title: What’s your AI game dev workflow? I keep losing interest once I start building
author: Ramirez_001
selftext:
Hey everyone,  
I’m a web developer, and honestly, I’ve been pretty tired of web dev lately. I started exploring game development with AI as a hobby, but I’m feeling stuck.

I keep getting excited about ideas, but once I actually start building them, I start losing interest. Something that sounded fun in my head doesn’t feel that interesting anymore when I try to turn it into a game. I end up going back and forth with AI, burning through a bunch of tokens, and still not really liking where the idea is going. It gets pretty discouraging.

I’m curious how other people here approach this:  
● What does your workflow look like, from coming up with an idea to making a small playable prototype?  
● How do you create assets and keep the art style consistent?  
● How do you decide whether an idea needs more work or whether it’s time to move on?  
● What do you usually get stuck on, and what helps you keep going?

I’d love to hear about your actual process, including the things that haven’t worked for you. I wanted this to be something fun to do as a hobby, but right now I’m struggling to find my footing.  
Does anyone else get stuck in this loop? What helped you get past it?

comments.author: Fuzzzy420
comments.body:
Totally normal behaviour I would say. 
Keep on it until an idea sticks, that's the one. 

If you have problems with consistency, make it your next project. Focus on one thing at a time

comments.author: TheFerret404
comments.body: First thing I do is make a detailed plan first chatting back and forth with opus 5.5 .. make the plan before your first prompt.. then I implement it in phases . When you go freestyle prompting it gets a mess fast. And for assets (3D) i let opus 5.5 take over blender trough mcp.. it can make decent low poly meshes, can rig them and everything. the freestyle prompting was really eventually the blockade for me.. because no oversight and messy code was not good for my adhd head 😂😂🤯

comments.author: Bavariasnaps
comments.body:
> I end up going back and forth with AI, burning through a bunch of tokens, and still not really liking where the idea is going. It gets pretty discouraging.

because you have a new kind of game mechanic in mind? Maybe try to change too much compared to already published games?

I used an established game mechanic, I know a story I want to tell and I get excited to to share it. with every update the game feels more alive. so maybe you are trying too much at the same time. have a good story, innovative game mechanics, implentings stuff that make it feel special, outstanding assets, good technical specs. all together its just too much. pick a few games you like and use their mechanics as an foundation.  you still can improve it and bring your own story and assets but storting from 0 is really difficult.

comments.author: yukajii
comments.body:
If you're a pro web dev it might not be as appealing to you, but I like going to dedicated ai game dev platforms like nanogram, astrocade, playgama etc where it's super easy to make a prototype right away and have at least some eyes on it. And browse around to see what people are into. 

If something you threw on a wall stuck - you can pick up from there and build it using more robust tools.

comments.author: ryan_umad
comments.body: you gotta play the game constantly. i have a playtest mode that screen records exactly what i’m doing, all my inputs, and my voice so i can just live narrate how i feel as i check out the latest tweaks and features. opus does a good job with creating new testable hypotheses , that i can then playtest. playtest playtest playtest. nothing is fun in theory, fun always comes down to practice

comments.author: KingofKingsofKingsof
comments.body: What's your game idea? If it is some big story that's not a game idea, that's a story. For both my games I basically started with a single level or room, and just worked on getting the basic gameplay being fun. One was a puzzle platformer, the other was a car combat game. The puzzle platformer involved not only making sure movement was fun but that the puzzle elements worked - that was a bit harder. The car combat game was mostly about the feel of the driving, thr enemy behaviour, etc. If the basic gameplay isn't fun then you won't have fun making it. As making it will mostly involve play testing it.

comments.author: Left-Prompt7557
comments.body:
For me, the fact that you are having loads of ideas, but some turn out to not be as fun as you first though, is a great thing and you should embrace it. I think one of the beautiful things about AI gamedev is that the speed of AI coding means you can be far more experimental and sacrificial with early ideas. It gives you the opportunity to try a bunch of things and see what sticks. Of course, then the tricky part is honing the bits that work.

In terms of my workflow, for the game I am developing, I'm using Unity with Claude Code in VSCode for the code. For the models I use human concept drawings or reference photos -> ClaudeCode -> ChatGPT -> Meshy API. This system more or less works for me (for now) and keeps token costs manageable, but I don't know if its the most efficient setup. That being said I think you can be too efficient with AI, sometimes a bit of managed workflow friction can be helpful, in so far as it can make you think more and be more creative in the way you do things, which can ultimately lead to more interesting stuff!

comments.author: imlo2
comments.body:
It's as normal as it can be;  working on anything you really don't know yet, and want to develop it will get you stuck, looking for solutions, get annoyed, frustrated, and you need to try again dozens of times, sometimes for weeks. The important thing to getting somewhere is if you can keep on pushing through that.   
That's pretty much the only factor that makes you someone who's a hobbyist, or a "real" developer/artist etc.   
  
And your questions; take one problem at a time, and look for what people have done earlier, and then start trying to crack your own specific issue. It doesn't matter if it's a workflow, art style, shader, animation, pathfinding logic or whatever it might be in a game, they are all problems to be solved.

comments.author: Horens_R
comments.body:
U come up with ideas by been creative or taking inspirations, there's no specific workflow as everyone's different to what brings them ideas. To test if it's good u simply test the core gameplay loop/mechanic or look at other examples that might've covered it already. 

"How to keep it consistent" 

> by making ur own

"When an idea needs work"

> by been a good game dev, not relying on ai n by playtesting extensively 

"What helps u keep going"

> The idea of making new and unique art for people to enjoy regardless of time, effort, popularity and money made from it.  When you start using ai you're often losing out on what make game dev a rewarding and enjoyable experience, you're skipping developing important skills for the sake of speed and immediate results. 

My comment may seem harsh, ai lowering the entry point is great n all but u need to have a willingness to create art in the first place. You have to try to learn the processes and skills rather than just copy and pasting.  For example if I try to code something but am completely stuck and can't find sources only then I'll ask ai for help. U don't jusy copy whatever it says, you take the time to digest it and experiment with the info it gives.

I like to give myself a to do list once I know what kind of game I'm making to keep me going. I write and draw down any thoughts I migh have, keeping a notebook handy at home or wherever u go is underated asf.

comments.author: Niedzwiedz87
comments.body:
In my case, I've been working on several small projects, some for work, some personal - in particular three games.

  
The first idea was exciting, and it managed to put me back in game development (I had practically abandoned many years ago due to lack of time for learning), but I realised my idea was overwhelming, even with the help of AI.

  
I decided to switch to a second idea that was not my main one, my most passionate one, because I thought I needed to learn, and I could give up on that project when I felt comfortable or bored, so I wouldn't have too much legacy design decisions to burden me.

  
I thought a lot about my third idea, I thought about my favourite games, what was in common, and I found the one thing I wanted dearly and I know I would enjoy playing. I've been working like crazy since end of September, and while there's still a lot of work, I have a game that is already fairly extensive, that can be fun, and that I feel motivated to keep working on. In fact I barely play games now, it's much more fun to work on this one, playtest, then change the game!

  
I think the three options are all valid, so pick your one:  
\- build to learn, with little expectations of success;

\- build as you go, maybe you'll figure it out, maybe you won't, but at least you're learning;

\- or plan it well but make sure it's something you love so dearly that you can stay motivated.

I've always had trouble finishing my projects, maybe I have a bit of ADD, but now with AI it's so easy to resume something even for a few minutes, rework systems that don't quite do what you want, it's exhilarating.

comments.author: FidoTheDogFacedBoy
comments.body: I’m kind of an explorer, I like to see what is possible and what I can learn how to do. I have to get pumped up for hard jobs. When I lose interest in something, I try taking a step down in tech level. I don’t arbitrarily remove features, I just reimagine how the completed project would look and feel using ai from a year ago, and remove those features. I keep taking steps down until I find something I can create within my interest window, and I build it and save it. When our build technology gets better, I’ll look at rebuilding my old ideas with features the ai has gotten better at building. Having a low tech prototype helps me find the most important features and the customer feels better having proof that I built something. I wish I had known this method when I first started programming.

comments.author: PettyPotatoJuror
comments.body: I get bored easily and have a lot of ideas. Now I have 20 projects that I just move between and move forward in increments. I am not sure if this is an ADHD type thing, but I've done it my whole life, it's just accelerated now with AI. I'd also note I don't have any need to make a career or living from what I'm making (although it's nice when hobbies pay for themselves) it's all just for my enjoyment, and if others like it, great.

comments.author: Ferniclestix
comments.body:
If you want to stay interested in making a game ive got a couple of things to say.  
\- Every day do something on it. add a health bar, make up a new attack, put rain on your main menu that drips down the buttons.  there are so many little things you can just say to an ai.  ad this little thing please.  
then you can go off and do your own thing.  your game will slowly grow even if you are a little bored of it.

\-prototype prototype prototype.  go to gemini, say i want a html game,  these are my mechanics, this is the game I want it like, this is the story line.  k go.   it will make you a functional protoytype, it might be terrible, it might need a tweak here or there but it might also get your creative juices going.  and you can do this whenever, you dont have to sit there and do the same game over and over. you can even excplore mechanics you arent sure about in a prototype , you dont have to put it in your main game.

you can make a chapter of any book into a game.   copy a big chunk of text that describes the world, some actions and a character. tell an ai to make it into a game.  it will do it.  lol

No game will ever be perfect, but any game can be fun, any game can have passion built into its core. if its something you can be passionate about then its somethign you can pay attention to, not sure if a toe clipping simulator would be fun?  prototype it.   a fishpoind on your desktop with the logos swiming around eating things(i did this one its funny as hell), little men that creep in when there is no mouse activity and start demolishing the desktop (also me,  my housemate was very annoyed lol)    there is so much you can do, even if its just to have fun makeing a little game just for you :)

dont put so much pressure on yourself to succeed.  games are for fun.

  
as for art, thankfully im trained in interactive animation for games so like... i know all the things, consistant art is really jsut a matter of you doing it, using a certain pallate and if your prompting AI art specifically  you want to learn how to use local models, then you want to set it up with your own set of lora, your own controlnet setup and then its you in control of the art.

when to move on is a hard one.  usually I weigh the gain from the time spent. if i judge its going to take a week to work out how to get font to display properly for my game, vs crappy blurry font... (true story) ill bite the bullet until it works.   if its like  do I ad 40 more ships 300+ weapons or do I just make six and let the users make thier own... i mean, six is so much less work!

all of thse questions are really relative to your own situation, your own abilities and your own interests man.  
I mean me, I cant program at all, nothing, nada, no html, no c++ no python, nothin, hell I struggle with math. but what I am good at is game design, game mechanics, animation, asset creation and knuckling down till ive beaten a problem into submission through sheer grind. 

theres not really a magic bullet for staying interested in things, if your not interested, find out what it is that does interest you and make it.  liek sonic? make sonic but different, add double jumps and devil may cry attack moves.  like wolfenstien but also earthworm jim?  make a 3d shooter but your just a worm trying not to die.     lol,  in this time, at this exact moment, you are not constrained by classic ideas of what a game is because you can just say to an ai. make this thing.

comments.author: Bonelessgummybear
comments.body:
I think because it's so easy to rapidly prototype, it's more important to playtest in grey box and make sure it's fun before doing too much. Build a demo, share it early, strangers will signal if it's worth continuing. But even then, it just takes 1 stranger to tell you how much fun they had playing and now you're motivated for at least another month.

I've made about 5 games for myself before sharing one I thought was fun. Now I'm pursuing a steam release

comments.author: Meatt
comments.body:
I just started (coded games before), and I'm using Deepseek Harness with an mcp connection to Godot. I haven't touched the code myself once, and I have a very serviceable prototype so far. Using Elevenlabs for sound effecis, music, and images. Those are both paid options, then I'm grabbing whatever free images I can from ChatGPT, and the new ComfyUI is way easier to use than it was before, so I'm trying to get some images from that as well.

For ideas, that's harder to give advice on. I've had some passion prototypes sitting around for years that I never finished, so I'm starting with those. Think of your dream game but with reasonable expectations and scope, then see what the AI can do. Usually it's the design and graphics that will need the most human time and effort.

comments.author: AsparagusOk8818
comments.body:
>I keep getting excited about ideas, but once I actually start building them, I start losing interest. Something that sounded fun in my head doesn’t feel that interesting anymore when I try to turn it into a game. I end up going back and forth with AI, burning through a bunch of tokens, and still not really liking where the idea is going. It gets pretty discouraging.

  
This is very normal.

The example I keep in the back of my mind is Dwarf Fortress: it took thousands of different little projects literally before the game we know as Dwarf Fortress had its foundations built. 

  
A few things that work for me: 

 \- Keep everything. Absolutely everything. Bored with a project and want to start fresh? Archive it. DO NOT THROW IT AWAY! Even if the fact that you are bored with it now has made you resent it, archive it. You will thank yourself later when you want to loot that archive for old systems, old assets, etc. Whatever your final project ends up being, a huge part of it almost certainly will be a chimera of those old archives. 

 \- Give yourself time before you start a new project. Don't just impulsively start something new. Have a food, maybe sleep on it, take a break. It might be that you're not actually bored of the project, just momentarily tired. 

 \- Allow your imagination and mind to explore a new idea without actually committing your hands to it right now. Have a different concept you like? Great - write it down, brainstorm it, put it aside. Maybe that's a later project. Maybe that's actually the real project, but not right now. 

 \- Come to peace with the fact that you will have to work through days on your project that will feel miserable and that you hate the project. It will happen. These days do not mean that you actually hate the project; they're just those days. They'll pass, and you'll feel excited about the project again. 

 \- If you play games while working on your game, try to stick to the same genre, even if you love multiple genres. I had to personally ban myself from playing any game that isn't the very same genre of game I am working on, because otherwise I'd start playing something and I would think, 'Oh, maybe a game like THIS game instead!' and then get all excited about a brand new concept, which was detrimental to the project. 

 \- The project is a journey. It is not some golden reward on a distant hill. The deep irony of all those shitty boilerplate ChatGPT 'My Journey' posts here is that they frame the journey as the thing that had to be overcome, now behind them, to get to the finish line. That's fckn backwards. If you think of the project as a bunch of tedious chores you need to tackle to get to the glorious end, your project is likely to fail and/or be terrible because you've missed the point of it. 

 \- Always remember that friction is part of the fun. A fun hobby would not be much fun, IMHO, if it were constantly easy and comfortable. 

 

To answer the specific questions:   


● What does your workflow look like, from coming up with an idea to making a small playable prototype?

Brainstorm (usually throwing a concept back and forth with ChatGPT, which usually results in something that sounds great in abstract, but then when trying to model it, it's atrocious. But that's actually fine because that's the heart of brainstorming - getting a rough approximation and then refining it) -> paper prototype (well, TTS prototype) -> initial Love game engine framework -> build towards fully playable level of the game -> if the fully playable level feels like it has the sauce, Git commit / if not, archive my work and take a break -> work on the Git-committed project and keep taste-testing the game 

I haven't yet made something I'd feel comfortable serving to anyone else, even as a little demo experiment, so I don't know what that will look like for me yet. 

  
● How do you create assets and keep the art style consistent?

Pixel sprite art, because it's easy to manipulate and the good pixel art tools are REALLY good (shoutout to Sprite Fusion and Pixel Lab), or I use ASCII art. 

Imagegen is a tempress and I'm sure she'll lure me back in, but the frontier models just aren't there yet, IMHO. People seem to be having some success with Meshy and/or Tripo, but that's not a world I'm ready to step into yet. 

  
● How do you decide whether an idea needs more work or whether it’s time to move on?

...Get out of the mindset of an idea being a meaningful thing. It isn't. Ideas are great during brainstorming, and then most ideas will fail during implementation. An idea does not need more work... like, how do you 'work' on an idea? A project needs work, and when you've started a project, then you are no longer working with ideas. You're working with systems, assets, architecture, etc. The conceptualization of your game as just an idea should not have survived prototyping.  
  
 For an asset or a system... I don't think there's any sort of easy rule for determining when to just move on or not. There's a pretty interesting story circulating right now about how GTA VI was experimenting with an alternative system to a weapon wheel, and it went through all sorts of iterations... and then, after months of work, they landed back on just using a weapon wheel. 

That kind of thing happens all of the time. It's just part of the process.

Something that probably IS a good general rule is not to overly attach yourself or overly commit yourself to a system or an asset. Something can be genuinely awesome, and yet you just can't find the right fit for it in your project. And that's okay - archive it. It will be useful later. 

It's also very useful to distinguish between the systems/asset vs how polished the project is. A system or asset can be great, but it feels wrong because it's not polished enough. This is where prototyping is both a trap and an invaluable thing to do - don't just prototype a system; prototype different ways of implementing that system, and also make sure you really dial in the ergonomics of your systems.

Great example: every modal window will feel like clunky garbage if the player can't dismiss it by just clicking outside of it. So a system that feels clunky/janky might not have any inherent problem; it's just trapped in a bad modal window that can't be intuitively dismissed.   


● What do you usually get stuck on, and what helps you keep going?

Content production gets me stuck. For me, it is always content production. 

I will have 4 extremely vivid concepts in my head; I will flesh them out... and the game will just need 10 more such concepts. And I don't have them. 

So I need to 'do my chores', as I call them, and set aside a day where I just build out the content that the game needs beyond the content I want it to have. 

When I first started doing these projects, I genuinely thought this was some kind of failure. Like I was just spinning my tires or whatever, or making filler for the game. 

But that's not true. The player has no idea what the stuff was that you had to invent secondarily, and they're just as likely to fall in love with it. Sometimes the inherent 'mystery' of a thing is what can make your world feel alive,  even if that 'mystery' is only there because you were frustrated filling in Enemy Type Number 9 and half-assed the job. I'll never forget the time I built a little tabletop game, and literally the night before I had friends test it, I realized I just needed another boss enemy. So I just quickly cobbled it together. I assumed I'd have to apologize for the one rushed piece of content.

That was everyone's favourite boss. 

Memories like that one are how I dig myself out of feeling like I'm just making filler or whatever when I'm doing my chores, and they make me question the value of what I'm doing.

A game will always be much more than the sum of its parts, and I think you need to be able to find a way to trust that whatever it is that is making you see the work as ugly at a given point, the sum of the game's parts will be much more than that ugliness.

comments.author: Careless_Road8873
comments.body:
Same loop hit me early on. I do web dev and have an office job, so every half finished game was another evening gone. A few things finally got me past it.

Pick a game you'd play anyway. Not a cool idea, something you'd actually open on a Sunday. When you're the player, the testing doesn't feel like work. Mine is a low fantasy survival game where you start as nobody with a few coins and try not to die. I've lost count of the hours I've spent playing it "just to check one thing".

Prototype ugly first. My first version was a plain HTML page with buttons. I only moved to Godot once I'd played it myself for a few days and still wanted more. If the ugly version isn't fun, art won't save it. That's also how I decide to drop an idea. If I'm not pulled back to the ugly version after a week, it goes.

For art, keep one fixed style block and attach one reference picture to every single prompt. Throw out anything that drifts, even if it looks great alone. Consistency beats quality. One off-style portrait breaks the whole screen.

Where I get stuck: Claude is great at logic and pretty bad at taste. It will write a whole battle system for you, then happily put twelve buttons on the first screen. So get people playing as early as you can and look at their screenshots, not your code.

comments.author: 7SINS_game
comments.body:
I actually went through this whole process recently.

I’m a hobbyist dev, and what started as a silly idea involving a bunch of leftover physical coins eventually turned into a complete iPhone strategy game.

My approach was pretty simple: build something playable, keep things as simple as possible (Occam’s razor), play it obsessively, figure out what doesn’t work, change it, and repeat.

AI helped enormously with development, but the actual game design decisions were always mine.

Two months later, my first game is approved for the App Store and launches next Friday.

My biggest takeaway? Make something you genuinely enjoy playing yourself. That kept me going through all the frustrating bits.

Whether anyone else will enjoy it remains to be seen. That’s the scary part. :-)

comments.author: amphivoice
comments.body:
If you want your art assets to look consistent you need to develop a single character art pipeline and art bible

Art bible: once you have got ONE thing in the game in the style you like, get your agent to do a dedicated art style milestone. Go back and forth until you like the style.

The agent can manage the pipeline once it's up and running but you need to spend time with the agent developing the pipeline if you want the art to look like it all came from the same place
